content.user_title: Build Python HTTP Clients with HTTPX
content.value_statement: Python services need reliable HTTP calls for APIs, streams, and authenticated integrations. This skill gives practical HTTPX patterns for sync, async, timeouts, streaming, and reusable clients.
actual_capabilities: Shows synchronous and asynchronous HTTPX request patterns for common API workflows.
Explains client reuse, connection pooling, timeout settings, and redirect handling.
Demonstrates Basic authentication, bearer tokens, custom headers, and custom auth classes.
Covers streaming downloads, streaming uploads, progress tracking, and large response handling.
Provides reusable API client patterns with context management and cleanup.
limitations: It provides guidance and examples, not a tested wrapper library or executable automation.
Real endpoints, credentials, retry rules, and error policies must come from the user.
Optional features such as HTTP/2 and WebSocket support require extra packages.
Version-specific behavior should be checked against the installed HTTPX release.

use_cases.title: Build Service API Clients
use_cases.description: Create HTTP clients with authentication, timeouts, status checks, and reusable connection settings.

use_cases.title: Stream Large API Responses
use_cases.description: Download large responses or files without loading the full payload into memory.

use_cases.title: Coordinate Async API Calls
use_cases.description: Use AsyncClient patterns to fetch multiple resources while keeping connection reuse and error handling clear.

prompt_templates.title: Make a GET Request
prompt_templates.prompt: Create an HTTPX example for a synchronous GET request to [endpoint]. Include status handling, JSON parsing, and timeout guidance.

prompt_templates.title: Send Async Requests
prompt_templates.prompt: Design an HTTPX AsyncClient approach for fetching several API resources concurrently. Include connection reuse and error handling.

prompt_templates.title: Add Authentication
prompt_templates.prompt: Show how to configure HTTPX for bearer token authentication, custom headers, and safe timeout settings. Keep credentials outside source code.

prompt_templates.title: Build an API Client
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a reusable HTTPX client for [service]. Include request methods, context management, retry guidance, streaming support, and cleanup.

output_examples.input: Plan a synchronous HTTPX request with timeout and error handling.
Convert sequential API calls to an async HTTPX pattern.
output_examples.output: A concise migration plan with client reuse, concurrent requests, exception handling, and result aggregation.

output_examples.input: Prepare a streaming download flow for a large file.

best_practices: Reuse Client or AsyncClient instances for connection pooling and lower request overhead.
Set explicit connect, read, and overall timeouts before calling external services.
Pass credentials from caller-managed configuration and avoid hardcoded tokens in source files.
anti_patterns: Creating a new HTTP client for every request in repeated workflows.
Reading large downloads into memory when a streaming response is available.
Copying placeholder API keys or example URLs into production integrations.

faq.question: What does this skill help build?
faq.answer: It helps build Python HTTP clients with HTTPX for sync requests, async requests, streaming, authentication, and timeouts.

faq.question: Does the skill run network requests automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides documentation and examples. Users choose the endpoints and decide when to run code.

faq.question: Can it help with asynchronous API calls?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes AsyncClient patterns for concurrent requests, connection reuse, and response handling.

faq.question: How should credentials be handled?
faq.answer: Keep credentials outside source code and pass them through secure configuration chosen by the application owner.

faq.question: Can it support large downloads?
faq.answer: Yes. It explains streaming responses so large payloads can be written incrementally.

faq.question: Does it cover WebSocket usage?
faq.answer: It references WebSocket support through the separate httpx-ws package, which must be installed separately.
